title: The oath before the gods
hookLine: the king swears by the son he loves, and the queen calls the sky to witness
carry: sakshi: a vow made before the gods
last: THE KING OWES YOU TWO BOONS.

cards: Dasharatha has had a wonderful day. The assembly said yes, the city is glowing, and tomorrow his favorite son becomes his heir.
He wants to tell the person he most enjoys telling things to, so he walks to Kaikeyi's rooms, which Valmiki describes as beautiful, full of birds and music and flowering trees. Her couch is empty.
A doorkeeper tells him, nervously, that the queen has gone into the anger room. And the king, happy a moment ago, goes cold.

teach.b: He finds her on the floor among her scattered jewels, kneels, and strokes her hair. Has someone insulted you? Tell me who.
Anything you want is yours. Kaikeyi asks him to swear first.
And Dasharatha, wanting only to see her get up off the floor, swears by the one he loves most. There's no one I love more than you, he says, except Rama, without whom I couldn't live an hour.
By Rama, I'll do what you ask. Now Kaikeyi makes the promise as public as she can.

teach.h: THE GODS ARE CALLED TO WITNESS.
teach.b: She calls the gods to witness: sun and moon, sky and earth, night and day, the household gods. She reminds him of the war with Shambara and the two boons, a vara each, a gift the receiver gets to choose. And she asks.

teach.h: BHARATA CROWNED. RAMA TO THE FOREST.
teach.b: Let Rama go to the Dandaka forest for fourteen years, in bark and deerskin, with matted hair. Why call the sky into the room? Because in Hinduism a vow isn't only between two people.
It's made before a sakshi, a witness, and the gods are witnesses who never look away.

teach.h: SURYA, THE WITNESS OF WHAT WE DO.
teach.b: Surya, the sun, is called karma-sakshi, the witness of what we do. It's why a bride and groom make their vows walking around the fire: Agni is the witness.

teach.h: SAKSHI: A VOW MADE BEFORE THE GODS.
teach.b: It's why a puja begins with a sankalpa, saying before God what you mean to do. Tonight Kaikeyi turns that holy habit into a trap, and the king learns what he gave away.

how: In Hindu rites a vow is made before a witness: Agni, the fire, at a wedding, and the deity at the sankalpa that opens a puja. Here Kaikeyi calls every witness she can name, so the king's word can't be quietly taken back.

o: two wishes the gods granted Bharata at his birth
two old gifts the king owed her, claimed to exile Rama
two curses Manthara laid on the king long ago

p: the witness at a Hindu wedding

s: Hindu couples walk around the fire because Agni is the witness to their vows
the fire is the sakshi, as Kaikeyi's sun and moon were for the king's oath.
the second boon sends Rama to the forest for fourteen years
in bark and deerskin, with matted hair.
the oath is made in secret
Kaikeyi calls the sun, moon, earth and gods to witness it.

games.q: at a Hindu wedding, the couple makes their vows walking around the fire. by today's teaching, why the fire?
o: for light, so the guests can see.
Agni is the witness; the vows are made before god.
to keep bad luck away from the in-laws.
games.why: Agni is the sakshi, the witness. like Kaikeyi's sun and moon, a vow made before the gods isn't just between two people.

practice: A puja often begins with a sankalpa, a short vow said before God. Try a small one. Think of one promise you mean to keep this week.
If you pray, say it quietly before God, or before a lit lamp; if you don't, say it under your breath to the morning. Breathe in, and feel the promise.
Breathe out, and feel how it changes once something has witnessed it: a little heavier, and a little steadier.

wordCard.voice: Kaikeyi's boons. Two gifts the king gave in gratitude years ago, claimed tonight with the sun and moon as witnesses: Bharata as heir, Rama to the forest for fourteen years.

orig.note: Sanskrit sākṣī: a witness. Kaikeyi calls the gods as witnesses; at a wedding, Agni is one.

carryVoice: Your line: sakshi: a vow made before the gods. Tomorrow, the longest night in Ayodhya. See you then.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda 10–11 (the king finds Kaikeyi; the oath by Rama; the gods as witness; the two boons asked)
